1) Bike sharing Data.

Source. https://www.kaggle.com/code/juniorbueno/rental-bikes/notebook

Data. The data contains the number of casual/registered users in bike sharing systems and various additional covariates (related to the weather) as well information on days/month/year.

instant: record index

dteday : date

season : season (1:winter, 2:spring, 3:summer, 4:fall)

yr : year (0: 2011, 1:2012)

mnth : month ( 1 to 12)

hr : hour (0 to 23)

holiday : weather day is holiday or not

weekday : day of the week

workingday : if day is neither weekend nor holiday is 1, otherwise is 0.

weathersit :

1: Clear, Few clouds, Partly cloudy, Partly cloudy

2: Mist + Cloudy, Mist + Broken clouds, Mist + Few clouds, Mist

3: Light Snow, Light Rain + Thunderstorm + Scattered clouds, Light Rain + Scattered clouds

4: Heavy Rain + Ice Pallets + Thunderstorm + Mist, Snow + Fog

temp : Normalized temperature in Celsius. The values are derived via (t-tmin)/ (tmax-tmin), tmin=-8, t_max=+39 (only in hourly scale)

atemp: Normalized feeling temperature in Celsius. The values are derived via (t-tmin)/(tmax-tmin), tmin=-16, t_max=+50 (only in hourly scale)

hum: Normalized humidity. The values are divided to 100 (max)

windspeed: Normalized wind speed. The values are divided to 67 (max)

casual: count of casual users

registered: count of registered users

cnt: count of total rental bikes including both casual and registered

Task. Fit a regression model to predict the total number of rented bikes (or, alternatively, the number of casual or registered users). Since the counts are relatively large, you may consider using the logarithm of the counts together with a Gaussian model. Discuss the impact of the different variables, paying particular attention to the presence of several categorical covariates. Perform model selection and include a prediction exercise.

2) Yacht hydrodynamic resistance

Source. UCI Machine Learning Repository, https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/243/yacht+hydrodynamics. Original record: Gerritsma, Onnink and Versluis, Geometry, resistance and stability of the Delft Systematic Yacht Hull Series, 1981.

Data. The dataset describes 22 different hull forms (sailing yacht), each tested at multiple Froude numbers in a towing tank, producing 308 hull-form \(\times\) Froude-number rows.

Variables:

LCB : longitudinal position of the center of buoyancy (% length).

prismatic : prismatic coefficient (dimensionless).

L_disp : length-displacement ratio.

beam_draught : beam-draught ratio.

L_beam : length-beam ratio.

Froude : Froude number (dimensionless, \(Fn = v/\sqrt{gL}\)), in [0.125, 0.45]. The dominant predictor.

resistance : residuary resistance per unit weight of displacement (target variable).

Task. The physics of the problem says that for sailing yachts the residuary resistance follows a power law of the Froude number with exponent close to 4 in the bulk regime. A good Bayesian project explores this:

  1. Log-log regression. Fit \[ \log(\mathrm{resistance}) = \beta_0 + \beta_F\,\log(\mathrm{Froude}) + \sum_k \beta_k\,\mathrm{hull}_k + \varepsilon\,. \] Verify that \(\hat\beta_F \approx 4\).

  2. BAS / BMA. Use bas.lm to enumerate the \(2^5\) submodels over the five hull-geometry covariates and identify which of them (LCB, prismatic, L/disp, B/draught, L/beam) carry signal once Froude is in the model.

  3. Correct for heteroscedasticity. Train the nonlinear model \[ \mathrm{resistance} = k\,\mathrm{Froude}^{\gamma_F}\,\exp\left\{\sum_k \beta_k\,\mathrm{hull}_k \right\} + \varepsilon \] where only the form factors that appear relevant in the model selection phase are kept for the nonlinear modelling. Compare the results with the log-log regression and discuss the impact of the heteroscedasticity correction on the inference on \(\gamma_F\) and on the hull-geometry covariates.

  4. Plot the posterior predictive curves and compare the curves with or without the treatment of the heteroscedasticity and compare the curves with the data.

rm(list=ls())
# Yacht hydrodynamics — UCI #243
yh = read.csv("data/yacht_hydro.csv")
dim(yh)
## [1] 308   7
head(yh)
summary(yh)
##       LCB           prismatic          L_disp       beam_draught  
##  Min.   :-5.000   Min.   :0.5300   Min.   :4.340   Min.   :2.810  
##  1st Qu.:-2.400   1st Qu.:0.5460   1st Qu.:4.770   1st Qu.:3.750  
##  Median :-2.300   Median :0.5650   Median :4.780   Median :3.955  
##  Mean   :-2.382   Mean   :0.5641   Mean   :4.789   Mean   :3.937  
##  3rd Qu.:-2.300   3rd Qu.:0.5740   3rd Qu.:5.100   3rd Qu.:4.170  
##  Max.   : 0.000   Max.   :0.6000   Max.   :5.140   Max.   :5.350  
##      L_beam          Froude         resistance     
##  Min.   :2.730   Min.   :0.1250   Min.   : 0.0100  
##  1st Qu.:3.150   1st Qu.:0.2000   1st Qu.: 0.7775  
##  Median :3.150   Median :0.2875   Median : 3.0650  
##  Mean   :3.207   Mean   :0.2875   Mean   :10.4954  
##  3rd Qu.:3.510   3rd Qu.:0.3750   3rd Qu.:12.8150  
##  Max.   :3.640   Max.   :0.4500   Max.   :62.4200
# The power-law in Fn is best seen on log-log axes (drop F=0 rows if any)
plot(log(yh$Froude), log(yh$resistance + 1e-3),
     pch = 16, cex = 0.5,
     xlab = "log(Froude)", ylab = "log(resistance)",
     main = "Yacht hydrodynamic resistance — power-law scaling")
abline(lm(log(resistance + 1e-3) ~ log(Froude), data = yh),

6) JFK Passengers

Source. https://github.com/alan-turing-institute/TCPD/tree/master/datasets/jfk_passengers

Data. The Port Authority collects monthly data on domestic and international passengers, cargo, flights, and aircraft equipment types from each carrier operating at PANYNJ airports.

Task. This dataset can be analyzed using a change-point model with different means before and after the change point, possibly including a linear drift after the change point. A basic model is \[ y_t = \mu_t + \epsilon_t, \] where \[ \epsilon_t \sim {N}(0,\sigma_t^2), \] and \[ \mu_t = \mu_1,\quad \sigma_t = \sigma_1 \qquad \text{if } t \leq \tau, \] while \[ \mu_t = \mu_2,\quad \sigma_t = \sigma_2 \qquad \text{if } t > \tau. \] Here \(\tau\) is an unknown change-point parameter.

More complex change-point models may also be considered and discussed. Time series models are encouraged; for example, one may include different trends and different variances before and after the change point.

9) SPF

Source. Federal Reserve.

Data. The Survey of Professional Forecasters (SPF) collects forecasts of macroeconomic variables. Both the U.S. SPF and the ECB-SPF ask forecasters to provide point forecasts and density forecasts. Density forecasts are reported in the form of histograms over a set of intervals specified in the survey instrument.

“H” horizon

“period” 0 corresponds to 10 bin, 1 to 11 bin

“YEAR” year

“QUARTER” quarter

“ID” forecaster id.

“INDUSTRY” forecaster type

“bin1” “bin2” “bin3” “bin4”
“bin5” “bin6” “bin7” “bin8” “bin9”
“bin10” “bin11” probability given to the bin (to be ignored)

“nbin_tot” number of bins used

“openL” “openR” 1 the forecaster gives positive probability to open (left/right) bin

“n.b.mode” position of the mode (wrt to bin number)

“prob.mode” probability assigned to the modal bin

“mode” value of the mode (unform model fitting)

“mean” value of the mean (unform model fitting)

“var” value of the variance (unform model fitting)

“median” value of the median (unform model fitting)

rm(list=ls())
GDP=read.csv("data/SPF_GDP.csv")
head(GDP)
GDP_B=GDP[GDP$QUARTER==1,]
Ydata=GDP_B[,c("mean","YEAR","ID")]  # select the variable of interest
hist(Ydata$mean,main="mean",xlab="SPF-GDP: mean")

Task. Investigate whether individual uncertainty appears to be associated mainly with respondent-specific effects, while point forecasts (e.g., mean or median forecasts) are more strongly affected by time-period effects.

In other words, the goal is to study whether there are substantial differences across forecasters in the confidence attached to their predictions, while each forecaster’s confidence evolves only slowly over time.

Consider only observations corresponding to a fixed forecast horizon (e.g., horizon 1, 2, etc.). If the variable of interest is denoted by \(y_{f,t}\) (for example, the forecast mean or \(y=\log(\sigma)\)), start with the model \[ y_{f,t} = \alpha_t + \beta_f + \epsilon_{f,t}, \] where \(\alpha_t\) represents the time effect and \(\beta_f\) the forecaster effect.

Compare variables related to point forecasts (e.g., mean or median forecasts) with variables related to uncertainty (e.g., variance or probability assigned to the modal interval).

More advanced models may also be considered. For example:

  • models with time-varying error variances;

  • mixture models in which forecasters are grouped into latent blocks, and responses depend only on the block membership.

Please ask the instructor for additional explanations if you are interested in this project.

10) Single-cell growth measurements

Source. Kennard, A. S., Osella, M. C., Javer, A., Grilli, J., Nghe, P., Tans, S., Cicuta, P., & Cosentino Lagomarsino, M. C. 2015. Individuality and universality in the growth-division laws of single E. coli cells. Physical Review E, 93, 012408 (ask the teacher for further details).

Data. The dataset cell_wide.csv contains single-cell morphological measurements collected from time-lapse microscopy experiments on a bacterial cell strian (P5ori) grown under two different culture conditions: Glc (Glucose) and RDM (Rich Defined Media). Each row corresponds to one observation of one individual cell at a given frame of the experiment.

Columns:

First column is an index uniquely identifying the cell under consideration.

medium: identifies the growth medium, either Glc or RDM.

t0, L0: time and length at birth (first frame of the cell’s life).

t1, L1, …, t61, L61: time and length at subsequent frames until the cell divides (last frame of the cell’s life).The final frame is not the same for all cells, hence the presence of trailingNA` values.

Task. For each cell, the length \(L\) typically grows exponentially between two divisions, that is \[ L(t)=L(t_0)e^{\beta (t-t_0)} \] where \(L(t_0)\) is the length at birth time \(t_0\) and \(L(t)\) is the length at time \(t\). Fit a model of the form \[ \log\!\left(\frac{L_i(t)}{L_i(t_0)}\right) = \beta_i (t-t_0) + \epsilon_{i,t} \] with independent Gaussian errors \(\epsilon_{i,t}\) and cell-specific coefficients \(\beta_i\). Study the distribution of the growth rates beta_i across conditions. Use hierarchical modelling to share information across cells and obtain more precise estimates of the growth rates. Discuss whether the two media GLC and RDM lead to significantly different cell sizes and/or growth rates.

11) Hourly city load factor

Source Salam & El Hibaoui, Power Consumption of Tetouan City, UCI Machine Learning Repository, https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/849/power+consumption+of+tetouan+city. The original release records the active power consumed by the three distribution zones of Tetouan (Morocco) during 2017, sampled every ten minutes by the SCADA system of the local utility.

Data. Data file: data/hourly_load_factor.csv (2000 rows). The CSV we share is a derived, pre-cleaned version. For each (day, hour) of the year we have computed the hourly mean of the city-wide active power \(\overline{P}(d, h) = \mathrm{Zone1}(d, h) + \mathrm{Zone2}(d, h) + \mathrm{Zone3}(d, h)\) from the original 10-min readings, and then the hourly load factor \[ \mathrm{LF}(d, h) = \frac{\overline{P}(d, h)}{\max_{h'} \overline{P}(d, h')}\,, \] i.e. the ratio between the average load in hour \(h\) and the highest hourly average of the same day. By construction \(\mathrm{LF}(d, h) \in [0, 1]\): the day-peak hour gets exactly \(1\) and the deepest off-peak hour gets the smallest value. From the full \(365 \times 24 \approx 8700\) (day, hour) cells we have taken a uniform random subsample of 2000 rows and clamped the values to \((10^{-3},\, 1 - 10^{-3})\) so that the Beta log-density is finite at the boundary.

Variables:

date : calendar date (M/D/YYYY).

hour : hour of the day, integer in \(\{0, \dots, 23\}\).

load_factor : hourly load factor as defined above, in \((10^{-3},\, 1 - 10^{-3})\).

Task.

  1. Compare a single Beta vs Beta mixture model with \(H = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5\), with model selection via WAIC.

  2. Overlay the posterior predictive density on the empirical histogram and verify that the modes are recovered.

  3. Post-hoc exploration. Assign each observation to its maximum-a-posteriori component, then plot the empirical fraction of observations in each component as a function of hour.

  4. Advanced. Fit a second model which does classification on hour using the component assignment as response variable, and plot the predicted probability of each component as a function of hour. Do the two plots match? Discuss the results. (Details for this step are presented in the additional details notebook) We will predict the component assignment using a multinomial logistic regression with the Fourier-transformed hour as covariate, i.e. with predictors \(\sin(k 2\pi h / 24)\) and \(\cos(k 2\pi h / 24)\) to capture the periodicity of the day.

rm(list=ls())
lf = read.csv("data/hourly_load_factor.csv")
dim(lf); head(lf); summary(lf$load_factor)
## [1] 2000    3
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
##  0.4257  0.5860  0.7329  0.7235  0.8042  0.9990
hist(lf$load_factor, breaks = 35, freq = FALSE,
     col = "tomato", border = "white",
     xlab = "Load factor (hourly / daily peak)",
     main = "Hourly city load factor — empirical density (n = 2000)")
lines(density(lf$load_factor, from = 0.01, to = 0.99),
      col = "darkorange", lwd = 2)

12) Capacitor accelerated life tests (survival data)

Source. Dataset capacitor from the R package survival.

Data. The dataset contains the result of 64 accelerated life tests on capacitors. The experiment follows a 4 x 2 factorial design over two stress variables:

voltage: the operating voltage during the test (4 levels);

temperature: the operating temperature during the test in degrees Celsius (2 levels — must be converted to Kelvin for the physical model);

time: observed time of failure (or censoring time), in hours;

status: censoring indicator (1 = failure observed, 0 = right-censored).

Task. A commonly used physical hazard model for capacitor failure is \[ h(t \mid V, T) \;\propto\; V^{\gamma}\,\exp\!\left(-\beta / T\right), \] with \(T\) measured in Kelvin. This corresponds to a regression on \(\log(V)\) and \(1/T\).

  1. Fit a proportional hazards model with linear predictor involving \(\log(V)\) and \(1/T\), and estimate the hazard ratio associated with each variable.

  2. Choose an appropriate parametric form for the baseline hazard, for example exponential, Weibull, or log-normal, and compare alternatives using information criteria such as DIC/WAIC, or posterior predictive checks.

  3. Extrapolate to typical conditions, namely \(50^\circ\)C and \(200\) V, which lie the experimental design, and obtain a posterior cloud or credible band for the survival function \[ S(t \mid V=200,\, T=323.15). \]

  4. (More advanced.) Compute the posterior distribution of the , i.e. the time at which 10% of the components have failed under operating conditions, namely \(50^\circ\)C and \(200\) V: \[ B_{10} \;=\; S^{-1}(0.9 \mid V=200,\; T=323.15). \]

rm(list=ls())
# install.packages("survival") #if needed
library(survival)
## Warning: package 'survival' was built under R version 4.4.1
data(capacitor)
## Warning in data(capacitor): data set 'capacitor' not found
head(capacitor)
dim(capacitor)
## [1] 64  5
# Convert temperature to Kelvin for the physical model
capacitor$tempK = capacitor$temperature + 273.15

# Quick look at the design
table(capacitor$voltage, capacitor$temperature)
##      
##       170 180
##   200   8   8
##   250   8   8
##   300   8   8
##   350   8   8
# Kaplan-Meier curves stratified by stress level
fit_km = survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ voltage + temperature, data = capacitor)
plot(fit_km, col = 1:8, xlab = "time (h)", ylab = "S(t)",
     main = "KM survival curves by stress level")
